Patras New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Patra, Greece

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Patras from Syria between 323-281 BCE; a 12th-century Romaniot community (per Benjamin of Tudela) grew substantially after absorbing Spanish and Sicilian refugees, peaking around 2,500 in 1569-70 as the region's largest Jewish community, then divided into Romaniot, Sicilian, and Sephardi congregations under several notable rabbis. Sephardi congregations disappeared by the early 17th century; Venetian conquests destroyed the community twice (1647 and 1684) before Ottoman recovery of the city allowed resettlement in the early 18th century. The 1821 Greek revolt drove most Jews to Larissa, Chalkis, and Corfu, leaving none by 1829. Corfu Jewish families reestablished the community in 1917, inaugurating a new synagogue in 1920 with Zionist activity; population reached 170 (of 64,838 total) by 1928, growing to 337 before WWII. Postwar recovery reached 122 by 1946, dwindling to just 5 by 1978. This newer cemetery's founding is unknown, most likely early 18th century.
